$schema-note: The mutant list, per unit, as data -- which is what closes Risk R13.
Every slice in the plan reports a mutation tally and none of them could be re-run: the mutants
were hand edits in a scratch worktree and were thrown away, so a tally was an assertion rather
than a measurement (Risk R13, plan section 6.145). A mutant here is a find/replace against one
ported file plus what it is EXPECTED to do, and `python tools/mutate.py` turns the tally back
into a command.
FIELDS.
unit.name     what to pass to --unit
unit.slice    the plan row this list belongs to
unit.filter   substrings handed to the test runner, one per TEST_CLASS that covers this
unit, so a mutant runs its own tests rather than the whole suite
unit.tests    how many tests those filters select, VERIFIED against the unmutated build
before any mutant is applied. A filter that selects the wrong tests reports
survivors for code it never ran, which is worse than no filter at all --
`hyperspace` was recorded as "Hyperspace" and matched three tests in other
files whose method names contain the word (plan section 6.147). The number
is a tripwire on the SELECTION, and the two directions do
not mean the same thing: a RISE is normally tests that did not exist when the
number was written, and is re-based here with the reason in the unit's note; a
FALL is a filter that has stopped reaching its own class, and is a bug
mutant.id     the name the plan uses for it, where the plan named one
mutant.find   text that must appear EXACTLY ONCE in the file; the run fails loudly if not,
because a mutant that silently applied nowhere is a mutant reported as caught
mutant.expect caught | survives | equivalent | uncompilable
mutant.selftest  true on the one mutant per unit whose job is to prove the HARNESS works --
an unmissable change the suite cannot fail to catch. A run in which a selftest
mutant survives is a run whose every other answer is worthless, and the tool
stops there rather than reporting a tally (Risk R13, plan section 6.119)
`expect: caught` is the normal case and anything else must say why in its note. A run fails
when an outcome differs from its expectation in EITHER direction: a new survivor is a gap in
the tests, and a recorded survivor that starts being caught is debt that has been paid and
should be written down as paid.

units.name: tactics
note: The ship AI and the autopilot (plan section 6.125). Both halves are closed: every `dock-*` and
`steer-*` mutation is caught after sections 6.131 and 6.132 found three branches its sweep could
not reach, and every `ta-*`, `msl-*` and `kill-*` mutation is caught after sections 6.152 and
6.153 closed the thirteen this file was written to record.
HOW THE FIFTEEN GOT HERE, kept because it bears on what the numbers below mean. The original
mutants were hand edits and are gone; what survived was their names in section 6.125. Each name
points at a constant or an operation that appears exactly once in `Tactics.cpp` -- `ta-253` at
the `CMP #253`, `msl-bit5` at the `BIT M32+1`, and so on -- so each edit below was reconstructed
from the name and from the routine, not recovered.
THE FIRST RUN, 2026-09-05, on the MSVC leg with a green 348-test baseline: 16 mutants, 3 caught,
13 survived. Thirteen survived exactly as section 6.125 recorded, which is the reconstruction
confirming itself thirteen times over; `ta7-three` and `msl-kill` came back caught and nothing
can now say whether those two reconstructions missed or that debt never existed.
THE SECOND AND THIRD RUNS, the same day: 16 of 16, none equivalent. Twelve of the thirteen were
the sweep -- six thresholds no seed stood on, a missile's whole arrival never executed, an
`ORA #104` reached by one odd value, a `CMP #16` whose branch read a bit no target had set, a
`TALLY` that was never compared, and a duplicate `TA20` that no missile in the port can reach.
THE THIRTEENTH WAS A DEFECT: `TA7`'s first `BCC` goes to `TA3`, which is part SIX, and the port
ran it into part five, so a ship above half its energy could launch a missile the original never
would. It was the LAST survivor closed, after three rounds of ladder-building had used up the
easy explanations -- which is the finding of section 6.153 and the reason a stubborn survivor
deserves more attention than a fresh one, not less.

mutants.note: THE HARNESS'S OWN OracleIsPresent for this unit. Dropping one of TAS6's three EOR #%10000000s leaves the negated vector wrong on the y axis, and TheNegationMatchesTAS6 compares all three against the shipped routine. Its job is to prove this run OBSERVES a catch -- without it, fifteen 'survivors' below could all be a harness that never rebuilt. Keep it first and never delete it.
The station's launch roll, three times in 256. Closed by a seed that reads 252 there.
The police roll. Closed by a seed that reads 239 there.
The Anaconda's escort roll. Closed by a seed that reads exactly 200 there.
TN7's random pitch, six times in 256. Closed by a seed that reads 249 and one that reads 255.

ORA #104 on the roll TN7 just made, reachable only through ta-250's branch -- and for a year one value reached it, 125, whose bottom bit is set. Closed by a seed that lands 252 at TN7 and then an EVEN operand (plan section 6.153).
Losing your nerve. Closed by a seed that reads 229 there.

TA7's first LSR A -- and its BCC goes to CAPITAL TA3, part SIX, so a ship above half energy skips the missile launch. THIS ONE WAS A DEFECT: the port ran both energy branches into part five. Closed by the fix plus three cases WITH missiles straddling the threshold (plan section 6.153).
TA7's second and third LSR A -- an EIGHTH of the maximum, not a quarter.
ta3's LDA ECMA / BNE TA3 stops a launch. ECMA was zero in every case that reached it; closed by a pirate with missiles and an ECM running.
TA20's EOR #%10000000, in SteerMissileTowardsTarget. A second, unreachable copy of TA20 stood in part 4 and was deleted (plan section 6.152).

TA64's CMP #16. Landing on 16 was not enough: the branch it guards reads bit 0 of the TARGET's INWK+32 and every missile in the sweep chased a slot whose byte 32 is even. Closed by a missile chasing slot 0 (plan section 6.153).
The station a missile dies against. Closed by cases that put the target at the missile's own position, which is the only way part 1's tail runs at all.
BIT M32+1 reads bit 5 out of the middle of an instruction. Closed by a victim marked in bit 4 and not bit 5, which is the only state that tells the two apart.
250 into OOPS when a missile arrives.

TA87's AND #%01111111 / LSR A -- the AI byte becomes the TARGET's slot for EXNO2. Not a coverage gap: TALLY and TALLYL were neither pushed nor compared, so what EXNO2 scores was invisible. Closed by comparing all three bytes (plan section 6.153).

units.name: hyperspace
note: The jump, witchspace and the galactic hyperdrive (plan section 6.136). Seeded with three
mutants rather than a full sweep, and they are here to prove the HARNESS rather than the
slice: two constants that a green suite must notice, and one recorded equivalent so the
'expect' field is exercised in more than one state.
A full list for this unit is work the next slice to touch it should do, and that is the
shape this file is meant to grow in: a slice adds its own mutants when it lands, instead of
reporting a number nobody can check.

mutants.note: THE HARNESS'S OWN OracleIsPresent. Inverting 'is this a space view' changes whether the hyperspace tunnel is drawn at all, so TheJumpMatchesTT18 cannot miss it. Its job is not to measure the port -- it is to prove that this harness still OBSERVES a catch, applies its edit to the file the build actually compiles, and rebuilds between mutants. Risk R13's realised form was a harness that reported catches it never saw (section 6.119); a run in which this one survives is a run whose every other answer is worthless. Keep it first in the list and never delete it.

CMP #253 / BCS MJP -- three jumps in 256 mis-jump, and `>=` to `>` makes it two. Survived every run until 2026-09-06 because the four seeds rolled 0, 104, 206 and 252, and 252 is one BELOW the boundary: the only value that separates the two operators is 253 itself. The roll is the first DORND from the seed, so the fifth seed was inverted rather than searched (plan section 6.156).

JSR CTRL / AND PATG / BMI ptg -- the cheat needs BOTH the key and the option. Survived because the sweep passed false for both and `&&` and `||` agree there. The test's own comment said the oracle could not answer `CTRL`; `CTRL` is `LDX #6` falling into `DKS4`, which on the C64 is `LDA KEYLOOK,X / TAX / RTS` over ordinary memory. All four combinations are a dimension of the sweep now (plan section 6.156). Re-anchored at M6-c-5, when `PATG` became `authorNames`.

A deliberate no-op: 0 and 0u are the same std::uint8_t. It is here so a run exercises the equivalent path, and it must never be 'caught' -- if it is, the harness is reporting on something other than the edit it made. Re-anchored by M5-a-10 (rule 3): the empty-tank clamp moved from Hyperspace.cpp into LightYearsTenths::Burned.

units.name: trumbles
note: MVTRIBS and the six Trumble sprites (plan section 6.148). Ten mutants, written with the
slice rather than reconstructed from a name, so this unit is a measurement from its first
run rather than a test of a reconstruction.
The two that matter most are `tr-carry2` and `tr-carry1`. The routine takes two random
numbers with DIFFERENT carries -- the first clear because an `ASL A` on a value below eight
cannot carry, the second set because `CMP #235` set it on the way past -- and the generator
reads C. Neither shows on screen; both move the whole sequence.
FIRST RUN, 2026-09-05, on the portable leg with a green 355-test baseline: 11 mutants, 9
caught and 2 survived. Both survivors were answered rather than recorded as debt.
`tr-leftsign` was a GAP and is closed: restricted to the 0 and 1 that MVTRIBS writes back,
the high byte of the x calculation can only come out as 0, 1, 2 or &FF, and &FF has every
bit set -- so bit 6 answers exactly as bit 7 does. Nothing in the library initialises
TRIBXH, TRIBVX or TRIBVXH, so the first pass after a Trumble appears reads uninitialised
RAM, and `TheSignTestReadsBitSeven` is that pass: all 256 starting values, which is where
the two bits disagree.
`tr-msb-or` is a PROVABLE EQUIVALENT and is recorded as one. See its note.
REWRITTEN 2026-09-05 when main's sprite work landed. `SPMASK` is no longer ported --
`VideoState` gives each sprite a whole sixteen-bit x, so the pair of masks that clear and
set one sprite's bit in a shared register have nothing to mask -- and `tr-spritebit` and
`tr-msb-or` went with it. `tr-sprite-index` and `tr-ninth-bit` cover the store that
replaced them.
THE COUNT WENT 8 -> 9 (M6-d-17). A filter is a substring of the whole `Suite.Method` name, so
this one also selects two tests outside the class by their METHOD names, and the second of
them -- `TheGameObject.ADockedPassBreedsTheTrumblesAndAsksForItsSyncs` -- arrived with T-2 on
the main track. It breeds trumbles, so the surplus is coverage rather than the `hyperspace`
mistake happening again.

mutants.note: THE HARNESS'S OWN OracleIsPresent for this unit. Dropping the y velocity leaves every Trumble on the row it started on, and TheYWrapMatchesMVTRIBS compares 768 rows against the shipped routine. Its job is to prove this run OBSERVES a catch; a run in which it survives is a run whose every other answer is worthless (Risk R13, plan section 6.119). Keep it first and never delete it.

The SECOND DORND's carry, which `CMP #235` set on the way past. Wrong here and the y velocity is drawn from a different entry of TRIBDIR about half the time AND the generator ends one state adrift, so the next frame's roll is wrong too. Nothing on screen would say so; TheDirectionChoiceMatchesMVTRIBS compares RAND.
The FIRST DORND's carry, which is the `ASL A` two instructions above -- clear, because A is at most 7. The mirror image of tr-carry2 and it fails on the same comparison.
`CMP TRIBCT / BCC` -- the pass on which the counter EQUALS the count must not move anything. Off by one and a hold with three Trumbles moves a fourth sprite that is not showing.
`AND #7` -- with three left it counts to three instead of seven, so a Trumble moves every fourth frame rather than every eighth and the sixth one never moves at all.
`CMP #235 / BCC MVTR1` -- the boundary itself. Told apart only by a seed that rolls exactly 235, and the direction sweep tries 256 seeds against six sprites.
`CMP #&50 / BCC oktrib` -- &150 exactly is off the right edge and &14F is not. The x sweep walks all 256 low bytes, so the boundary is in it by construction.

`BPL nominus` reads bit 7 and nothing else. SURVIVED on the first run, because within the 0 and 1 that MVTRIBS writes back to TRIBXH the high byte can only be 0, 1, 2 or &FF and &FF has bit 6 set as well. Closed by `TheSignTestReadsBitSeven`, which sweeps all 256 starting values of TRIBXH -- not an invented state, because nothing in the game initialises that byte and the first pass reads whatever the loader left.

`LDA #&48 / STA T` -- where a Trumble that walked off the left edge reappears. &48 rather than &50 is not arbitrary: at &150 the very next test would decide it had gone off the RIGHT edge and send it to zero, so this mutation makes the sprite teleport to the left edge instead of the right one.

The Trumbles are VIC-II sprites 2 to 7, not 0 to 5 -- sprites 0 and 1 are the laser sights and the explosion. Dropping the offset moves the wrong two sprites and leaves the top two Trumbles still, which the whole-register comparison sees on the first case.

The ninth x bit, dropped on the way into the register. This is the store that REPLACED `ORA SPMASK+1,Y / STA VIC+&10`: `VideoState` holds a whole sixteen-bit x, so the read-modify-write of a shared byte became one write, and this is the mutant that proves the second half of it is still there. A sprite past column 255 would sit on the left of the screen instead.

units.name: missions
note: The four control codes a mission briefing is made of (plan section 6.149).
TWO OF THESE ARE ABOUT A FALL-THROUGH. `PAUSE` ends `JSR LL9` and the next instruction is
MT23's `LDA #10`, so a briefing's `{22}` moves the cursor to row 10 and forces lower case as
surely as a `{23}` does. The port splits that across two objects -- the row is the seam's and
the two case flags are the text system's -- and the mutants below take one half away each.
FIRST RUN, 2026-09-05: 12 mutants, 9 caught, 3 survived, and all three were real gaps in the
sweep rather than debt. `mi-release` needed a keyboard that starts with a key DOWN;
`mi-mt9-view` needed a token that is not 216; `mi-pause2-loop` needed a scan count that does
not wrap -- and the mutant itself was replaced, because `if (x) continue;` at the top of a
`for(;;)` and `while (x) {}` are the same loop, so the first version could not have failed.
SECOND RUN, 2026-09-05, with 4d-c's thirteen added: 25 mutants, 22 caught, 3 survived, and all
three are recorded equivalents. `mi-mt9-view` became one: it was written as a defect and the
run proved the defect had no effect, because `TT66` writes the same `XC` twice on its own.
THE COUNT WENT 9 -> 12 (M6-d-17): `TheMissionText` grew from six tests to nine after the nine
was recorded. The three in `TheMissions` were counted then and are counted now.

mutants.note: THE HARNESS'S OWN OracleIsPresent for this unit. Putting the briefing ship at z_hi = 0 rather than 2 draws it at a two-hundredth of the distance, which the whole-canvas comparison in TheBriefingShipMatchesPAS1 cannot miss. Keep it first and never delete it.

The byte the upstream comment gets wrong. `PAS1` on this build is `LDA #2 / STA INWK+7`; the Master and Apple versions load 1 and the comment was written for those. A port that trusted the comment would put the Constrictor at half the distance and twice the size, and this is the mutant that says so.
`conhieght`, which the source calls the size of a gap and which is really the ship's y coordinate. One row out is a whole-canvas difference.

The FIRST of PAUSE's two loops, dropped. `JSR PAS1 / BNE PAUSE` waits for the player to LET GO of the key that turned the previous page; without it one keystroke dismisses every remaining page of a briefing in a single frame. SURVIVED the first run, because the sweep always started with an empty keyboard and the loop is invisible from there -- closed by giving the script a `held` run, which is the state the loop exists for.
`LDA #0 / STA INWK+31` -- the ship stops being drawn, so the `LL9` after the screen change has nothing to rub out. Leaving the flags set makes that `LL9` erase lines the cleared screen no longer has.

The row PAUSE's fall-through moves to. MT23 loads 10 and MT29 loads 6, and the `EQUB &2C` between them is what makes the two one routine -- so this is the mutant that proves the port fell through into the right entry point.

PAUSE2's `BEQ PAUSE2` goes back to the TOP of the routine and not to the scan above it, so an empty second scan re-checks for a release the routine has already had. The mutant turns that into a do-while, which is the reading everybody has first. It shows only when the keyboard goes empty, empty, PRESSED: the real routine treats that third scan as 'still held' and goes round again, and the do-while takes it as the answer. Two scans apart, and nothing is drawn, so the scan count is the only instrument -- which is why the script counts calls in a byte that cannot wrap. The first version of this mutant was `continue` against an inner `while`, and those two ARE the same loop.

MT27 and MT28 swapped. The two ranges are three apart and OVERLAP, so galaxy 3's captain is galaxy 0's planet -- which means a swap is invisible for exactly one pair of inputs and visible for the rest. The sweep covers all eight galaxies of both.

`CLC / ADC GCNT` dropped, so every galaxy gets galaxy zero's captain. This is what the fixture itself did for an afternoon, by poking `GCNT` before `Mirror` overwrote it with the commander block -- `GCNT` is `TP+15`.
The token `BRIS` prints. 216 is INCOMING MESSAGE and 215 is a carriage return, so this is the mutant for a briefing that opens on a blank screen.
`LDY #100 / JMP DELAY` -- two seconds on PAL. Compared as a number rather than as elapsed time, because neither side has a raster.

MT9's column store, DROPPED -- and it makes no difference, which is not what this mutant was written to show. `LDA #1 / JSR DOXC / JMP TT66` is one load serving as a column and a view, and the port had only the view; adding the store is faithful and is what the routine does. But `TT66` sets `XC` to 1 ITSELF, twice -- once near the top and again at `.tt66 LDX #1 / STX XC / STX YC` -- and nothing between `DOXC` and `TT66` reads the byte, because `JMP TT66` is the next instruction. So the `DOXC` is DEAD, and the port was accidentally right for two slices. Recorded as an equivalent, with the store kept: it is the FIFTH piece of dead code found in the original, after `cntr`'s `REDU`, `.OLDBOX`'s cursor store, `MAS2`'s second entry and `TITLE`'s `LDA MCNT / AND #3`. It must never come back caught -- if it does, something has stopped writing `XC` in `TT66`.

The shift-set-rotate trio sets bit 0; clearing it instead means the Constrictor is offered for ever. The sweep starts from sixteen values of TP so the flag is compared from states where it was already set as well as from states where it was not. Re-anchored at M6-d-29, when the comment inside the `find` lost its listing.

`BRIEF3`'s `AND #%11110000`, dropped. Picking the plans up also FORGETS mission 1 -- both its bits go -- and a port that only ORed would agree from every starting state whose low nibble was already zero, which is why the sweep walks sixteen of them.

`LSR TP / ASL TP` clears bit 0 and LEAVES BIT 1, which is what takes the pair from `%11` to `%10` -- finished and paid, and never offered again. Clearing both would leave it at `%00`, which reads as never started.

5,000 CREDITS IS 50,000 TENTHS. The cash is held in tenths of a credit throughout, so a reward written in credits pays a tenth of what the game pays -- and the whole commander block is compared, so it is the four cash bytes that say so.
`LDA #2 / STA ENGY` -- the navy's energy unit, which the flight loop reads as three units a pass where the shop's one gives two. A 1 is the shop's.
`INC TALLY+1` -- the HIGH byte, so the reward is 256 kills and a whole combat rank rather than one kill. This pair is low byte first, unlike the cash above it, which is exactly the trap.

Bit 4 set AFTER the question rather than before it. In the game the order matters -- `BCC BAYSTEP` leaves before the `INC` -- but the flag is set above the `DETOK` and nothing between the two reads it, so moving it past a print that cannot fail is the same program. Recorded as an equivalent so a run exercises that path, and it must never come back caught.
`INC TRIBBLE` -- the player leaves with ONE Trumble and `MLOOP`'s breeding does the rest. Two would double every population the game ever reaches.
`LDA #64 / STA MCNT` -- how long the Constrictor turns before it starts to move away. One frame out is a different screen and a different `MCNT` at the end, and both are compared.

mutants.replace: // 6502: the ship climbs one row a frame
mutants.note: The SECOND `INC INWK+6 / BEQ BR2` of the pair. The ship recedes two units a frame and the loop can end on either half, so dropping one halves the speed and changes which frame the briefing appears on. Re-anchored at M6-d-29, when the comment inside the `find` lost its listing.

`CPX #conhieght / BCC P%+4 / LDX #conhieght` clamps at the value rather than above it, and `>=` against `>` is the same clamp: the only value they treat differently is `conhieght` itself, which both leave at `conhieght`. An equivalent by construction, kept so the run exercises one.

`DEC MCNT` in the SECOND loop, which nothing branches on. The counter is live in the first loop and dead in the second, and dropping it there is invisible on screen -- so `MCNT` is compared as state, which is the only place it shows. Re-anchored at M6-d-29, when the comment inside the `find` lost its listing.
`.BR2 INC INWK+7` -- the high byte following the low one past 255. Without it the ship is 256 units nearer than the briefing text was written for, and `INWK` is compared byte for byte.

units.name: raster
note: COMIRQ1's VIC-II half (plan section 6.155). Written with the slice, so this unit is a
measurement from its first run rather than a test of a reconstruction.
FOUR of the handler's six registers reach the screen and they are two effects. `moonflower`
and `welcome` are the energy bomb; `santana` and `lotus` are how the explosion sprite is kept
out of the dashboard, which is a colour change rather than a clip. The other two -- `shango`
and the memory pointers -- are programmed correctly and consumed by nothing, so only the
oracle's write-ORDER comparison can tell a right value from a wrong one there. That is why
the comparison is a sequence and not a final state.
`ra-blit-per-sprite` is the one mutant outside `Raster.cpp`, and it is here rather than in a
canvas unit because what it breaks is this routine's output being read per screen row.

mutants.note: THE HARNESS'S OWN OracleIsPresent for this unit. Zeroing the raster line the next interrupt fires on is a register the comparison reads on every one of 256 passes, so a run in which this survives is a run whose every other answer is worthless (Risk R13, plan section 6.119). Keep it first and never delete it.

BIT BOMB / BPL reads bit 7 and nothing else. The sweep runs the bomb byte at 0, &80, &7F and &FF, and &7F is the one that tells this bit from any other: every bit but the top one set, and the flash must not start.

welcome,X, and which half reads which byte. Taking the fixed one for both halves means the space view never flashes -- the bomb's whole visible effect below the mode change -- and the oracle's VIC+&21 write says so on the pass the port got wrong.

INC welcome sits ABOVE the split test, so both passes reach it and the colour moves twice a frame. This mutant is the plausible mistake -- incrementing only on the pass that shows it -- and it halves the flash rate. Caught on the dashboard pass, where the oracle's welcome has moved and the port's has not.

innersec is what makes the split alternate: a handler that left RASTCT where it found it would program one half of the screen for ever. TheSplitAlternates is the assertion, and the oracle comparison reads RASTCT back on every pass as well.

zebop is a CONSTANT and abraxas is state, which is the whole reason that pair is not a table. Reading the variable for both halves would colour the space view from the dashboard's block whenever the dashboard is up -- invisible in the port today, because Resolve takes the upper half's block as fixed, and caught only by the oracle's VIC+&18 write.

lotus read the wrong way round: VIC+&28 is SPRITE 1's colour, so this swaps the explosion's red into the dashboard half and its invisibility into the space view. Caught by the oracle's write order AND by the two compositing tests, which is the point -- until slice 4f this register reached nothing and only the first would have.

santana, which differs between the halves in exactly one bit -- sprite 1's. Taking the space view's mask for both halves leaves the explosion multicolour over the dashboard, which is the defect the port had before 4f read the register at all.

Deciding a sprite's mode once instead of per screen row. The VIC-II decides it as it scans, which is why a burst that straddles the split is drawn on one side only; pinning the half to the space view's draws the whole thing over the dashboard. Re-anchored at Resolution.md RS-0, when `BlitSprite` took the output's split row as a parameter so that one blit serves the canvas and the 640x400 picture.

units.name: cloud-seed
note: The EE55 cloud seeding, the carries it reads and the two defects the tightened comparison
found beside it (plan section 6.157). Every decision here is a flag: which carry the first
DORND rolls in, what the other three get, what EE51 leaves, what ANGRY leaves, what the
scooped canister's roll gets. Each mutant flips one and names the oracle test that sees it.
THE COUNT WENT 17 -> 18 (M6-d-17): M6-a-1 added `TheFlightFrameShips.TheDockingChecksMatchISDK`
while closing the fourth coverage gap.

mutants.note: THE HARNESS'S OWN OracleIsPresent for this unit. Byte 2 is the vertex count DOEXP loops down from; zero is the unseeded value that wrote 250 bytes across the neighbouring heaps, so TheCloudSeedsLikeEE55 sees the byte and TheWreckageStaysInsideTheSpaceView sees the corruption. Keep it first in the list and never delete it.

CPY #6 / BNE EE55 -- Y is under six on the way round, so the second, third and fourth DORND roll in a CLEAR carry whatever the first one had. Feeding them the first one's flag agrees on the clear-carry cases and not on the set-carry ones; TheCloudSeedsLikeEE55 runs both.
LL155's CMP #4 / BCC LL82 -- a heap with no line on it leaves the carry CLEAR, and ErasingAShipMatchesEE51 runs an empty heap against the oracle's exit flag.
LDA #18 -- the counter DOEXP ages, and the CPY #18 that decides the burst sprite's one frame reads it. TheCloudSeedsLikeEE55 compares heap byte 1.

.oily JSR DORND reached only by CPX #OIL / BEQ oily, and an equal compare SETS the carry. This was the port until 2026-09-06, hidden while the comparison skipped the generator on frames that seeded a cloud; ThePerShipLoopMatchesMAL1's 'on top of us with scoops' compares RAND now.
CMP #SST with the station itself in A leaves the carry SET (equal), and BEQ AN2 returns on it. TheAngerMatchesANGRY compares the exit flag on every case, and a third of them call with the station.

mutants.find: carry = true; // 6502: the flag `HITCH` sets, which nothing on the way to `MA47` touches
mutants.replace: carry = false; // 6502: the flag `HITCH` sets, which nothing on the way to `MA47` touches
mutants.note: HITCH's SEC is the flag JSR LL9 gets for a ship in the sights with no missile armed and no laser firing, and a ship that arrives there killed and not on the screen seeds its first DORND on it. ThePerShipLoopMatchesMAL1's 'in the sights, already dead' is that ship, and its RAND is compared -- 'on top of us' is not, because MVEIT takes the player's speed off z before HITCH looks, and the generator was not compared by the frame tests until this mutant survived (2026-09-06).

units.name: rng
note: `DORND` (plan section 6.1). Thirty-nine lines, and every byte the game rolls comes through them, so a
slip here is invisible to every test that compares an outcome and visible only to the one that
compares the generator's own four bytes. M6-0-g put mutants on the two carries the routine
threads: the one between its halves, and the one the caller arrives with.

mutants.note: THE HARNESS'S OWN OracleIsPresent for this unit. The fourth state byte takes the new value instead of the old one, and every sequence comparison sees it on the second call. Keep it first.

mutants.find: const AddResult main = AddWithCarry(previous, partner, feeder.carry);
mutants.replace: const AddResult main = AddWithCarry(previous, partner, false);
mutants.note: The feeder half's carry is what the main half adds in; dropping it leaves a generator that is right for a while and then one out. Would have hidden: every downstream table, spawn and stardust field drifting from the shipped game after the first carry.

The carry the caller arrives with is an operand -- DORND2 exists because it is. Forcing it clear makes every DORND a DORND2. Would have hidden: every section-6.121-shaped finding, where a caller's flag state is what the port got wrong.

units.name: arith
note: The arithmetic kernel (plan section 6.2 onwards), compared exhaustively or over sweeps. Three of the
four mutants are dropped flags, because a dropped flag is what this file's history is made of:
`MU1`'s `CLC`, `ADD`'s exit carry and `LL5`'s last `ROL` are each read by a caller that does
nothing to set them itself.

mutants.note: THE HARNESS'S OWN OracleIsPresent for this unit. Seven shift-and-add steps instead of eight leaves every product a bit short, and the exhaustive MULTU sweep cannot miss it. Keep it first. Re-anchored at M6-c-7, when the kernel's scratch letters took names.

mutants.find:
// drops, and it is what stops a zero multiply looking like an overflow to the caller below.
      return Product{0, 0, false};
mutants.replace:
// drops, and it is what stops a zero multiply looking like an overflow to the caller below.
      return Product{0, 0, true};
mutants.note: `MU1` is `CLC / STX P / TXA / RTS`: a zero multiplier clears the carry as well as both halves. Would have hidden: a zero multiply reading as an overflow to the three callers that take the carry before setting it.

`ADD`'s same-sign path leaves the carry `ADC T1` produced and `ORA T` does not touch it. Would have hidden: a caller whose next `ADC` runs on the addition's carry getting a clean one instead. Re-anchored at M6-c-7, when the kernel's scratch letters took names.

`LL5`'s exit carry is the last `ROL A` before `DEC T / BNE / RTS`, and `SUN` hands it straight to `DORND` (plan section 6.55, the tenth dropped flag). Would have hidden: the sun's ragged edge seeded from the wrong bit. Re-anchored at M6-c-7, when the kernel's scratch letters took names. M6-c-7 re-anchored the `find` and left the `replace` naming `q`, so the mutant stopped compiling instead of running; M6-d-17 finished the job, which is the first full harness run since.

units.name: shipmove
note: `MVEIT` and what it calls (plan sections 6.33 to 6.38). The mutants sit on the three places the port
was wrong first time or the original is not what it looks like: the inverted `BPL MV43`, the
`ADC` with no `CLC` under it, and `TIDY`'s loop that stops one byte short.

mutants.note: THE HARNESS'S OWN OracleIsPresent for this unit. Speed times two instead of four moves every ship half as far along its nose, and twenty iterations of MVEIT see it on the first. Keep it first.

`BPL MV43` branches to the SUBTRACTION when the signs agree, the opposite way round from every other sign test in the file. Would have hidden: the y coordinate one out on the first iteration, which is how the port's first reading was found. Re-anchored at M6-c-4, when `BET2` became `pitchSign`. Re-anchored at M6-c-9, when `MoveShip`'s `K2` became `rolledY`.

EQUIVALENT, AND PROVABLY SO. `LDA P+1 / ADC K2+1` has no `CLC` and runs on the carry `MLTU2` left -- but that carry is ALWAYS CLEAR. `MLTU2` opens with `LSR A / STA P+1`, so bit 7 of P+1 is zero, and its sixteen `ROR P+1 / ROR P` pairs shift exactly that bit out on the last one; `WideMultiplyMatchesOverASweep` counts the carries the shipped routine leaves over 150,000 samples and asserts the count is zero. The mutant replaces a flag that is never set with `false`, so it survives, and the ADC-without-CLC the port reproduces is safe for a reason rather than by luck. First run 2026-09-07: survived, as an equivalent must. Re-anchored at M6-c-9, when `MoveShip`'s `K2` became `rolledY`.

`TIL1` counts X down in twos from 14 and stops at INWK+23, so the side vector's z_lo survives the tidy. Clearing it too is the obvious port and the wrong one. Would have hidden: an orientation byte the original keeps and the port threw away.

units.name: planetdraw
note: `PLANET`, `SUN`, `CHKON` and `ZINF` (plan sections 6.40 to 6.57). The mutants are the clamp
`PL82` writes, the branch `CHKON` takes to `PLS6`'s `CLC` rather than `EDGES`'s (section 6.45), and
the middle of `SUN`'s three roughness thresholds.
The filters overlap on purpose: `ThePlanet` also selects `ThePlanetLineHeap` and `TheSun` selects
`TheSunLineHeap`, so the twenty-one the tool counts are twelve tests, some run twice. The
filter gate caught the first record of twelve, which is what the gate is for.
THE COUNT WENT 21 -> 24 (M6-d-17). `PicturePlanetTests.cpp` arrived with RS-3 on the main track
and its three tests are selected by their METHOD names: two contain `ThePlanet` and one
`TheSun`. They put the planet and the sun on both surfaces, so the surplus is coverage.

mutants.note: THE HARNESS'S OWN OracleIsPresent for this unit. `ZINF`'s nose sign is what makes a new ship face the player; without it the cleared block differs in one byte and the block comparison says so. Keep it first.
A radius that overflowed a byte is clamped to 248, not 255, and K+1 is left set for `PL9`. Would have hidden: a close planet drawn seven pixels too wide.

mutants.find: return extent; // 6502: PL44 -- which is `PLS6`'s carry clear, not `EDGES`'s (§6.45)
mutants.replace:
extent.offScreen = true;
      return extent; // 6502: PL44 -- which is `PLS6`'s carry clear, not `EDGES`'s (§6.45)
mutants.note: A circle whose top is above the screen is ON screen -- `BMI PL44` lands on a `CLC`, not on a rejection (plan section 6.45). Would have hidden: a planet vanishing the moment its top edge left the view.
`CPX #40 / ROL A` is the middle of the three thresholds that make `CNT` 0, 1, 3 or 7. Would have hidden: a sun between 40 and 47 wide drawn with a smoother edge than the shipped one.

units.name: spawn
note: `NWSPS`, `KILLSHP`, `SOLAR`, `ze`, `FRS1` and `SFS1` (plan sections 6.58, 6.117, 6.121). Two of the
mutants are the two carries into `DORND` that the port got wrong before the oracle corrected it,
and the third is the Dodo's tech-level threshold.

mutants.note: THE HARNESS'S OWN OracleIsPresent for this unit. The station's roll counter at 127 instead of 255 is one byte in the block NWSPS is compared on. Keep it first. Re-anchored at M6-d-25, when the comment beside it lost its listing.

`ze` has no RTS: it falls into `DORND2`, whose `CLC` is what the second roll rotates in, whatever the `ROL A` above shifted out (plan section 6.117). Would have hidden: the generator one bit off after every debris block.

The carry into `SFS1`'s `DORND` is SET every time, because reaching it means `CMP #PLT` did not borrow and `PHA` leaves the flag alone (plan section 6.121). The port had `false` here once. Would have hidden: every tumbling canister's spin and speed.
`CMP #10 / BCC notadodo`: tech level 10 gets the Dodo. Would have hidden: a Coriolis at exactly the level that earns the other station.

units.name: flight
note: `RESET`, `RES2`, `ZERO`, `TT110`, `TITLE` and `DEATH` (plan sections 6.94 to 6.108). The mutants
are the two findings in the reset pair -- `RES2` re-centres the pitch and not the roll, and
`RESET`'s seven zeroed bytes are this build's, not the BBC's -- and the station's launch position.

mutants.note: THE HARNESS'S OWN OracleIsPresent for this unit. `RESET`'s energy is the same 255 that means docked; one less is one byte off in the flight state the reset test compares. Keep it first.

`STA JSTY` is in `RES2` and `STA JSTX` is not, and neither is inside `ZERO`'s range: a launch inherits the last flight's roll. Re-centring both is the natural port. Would have hidden: the roll rate a launch starts with.

`LDX #6 / STA BETA,X` clears seven bytes from `BETA`, and in this build the third is `QQ22+1`, the hyperspace countdown -- the BBC's layout at those addresses is the text cursor. Would have hidden: a countdown surviving a reset.
`INC INWK+7` once: the station you have just left is one high-byte unit behind. Would have hidden: the station spawned twice as far away on every launch.

units.name: game
note: `Elite::Game` (Modernize.md section 4.4) -- the object that calls the routines every other unit
compares. Nothing here is arithmetic; what a mutant catches is a CALL left out, which is the shape
of every outer-loop defect the plan's section 6.128 and 6.111 record: a routine ported, swept, green
and reached by nothing. InputTimer.md T-2 added the first, on the docked pass reaching `MLOOP`'s
part 5 whole rather than its two countdowns alone.
